articles.title: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons
articles.summary: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons

top_comments: Dang, the prices are crazy. $10k for the lowest tier? I expect federal data to be free. Most federal data related to stuff like regulation (e.g. FCC spectrum use coverage maps), maps for federally-managed lands, etc. is free. And, it should be free. It's a core part of accountability and transparency. Historically there was a copying cost (having a human print physical copies on paper or CD/DVD/tape), which is understandable, but now that the incremental cost of each new copy approaches $0, that's what it should cost users of the data.

I thought these were going to be free and got so excited.FWIW if you're willing to deal with some 'fuzziness' and the occasional missing zip code that's commercial only, the ZCTA shapefiles are free and are close enough for many purposes: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/g...

This is interesting. For a long time it was pointed out that ZIP codes, unlike say, city or state boundaries, were not properly representable as polygons, since they don't divide up acreage into zones, but rather label postal delivery routes. Suppose I build a new neighborhood way out in the middle of nowhere. The "polygon" concept suggests that we could look and see what polygon I'm in, and that will determine what post office delivers my mail. But in reality, if there was no route to that area already, they could decide to make it part of any one of the surrounding routes.I suppose though, as long as you let the polygons map has uncontained areas, where no routes currently exist, it's a doable task to draw polygons around the limits of every route network, as long as you don't mind that they may have lots of weird ragged edges.

articles.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
articles.summary: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators

top_comments: Note that this is specifically Consumer Gemini with Connected Apps; Workspace Gemini (and Workspace Intelligence, the RAG thing for enterprise/Workspace) still claims not to be subject to human review:https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/generative-ai/g...So basically if you use consumer Gemini and specifically authorize the GMail app, for example, then it will sometimes use the GMail tool to load your mail from GMail, and that data (like all data in consumer Gemini) might be given to the human annotation pipeline.This whole thing seems deeply stupid to me from Google's standpoint, although they've never been good at product management - there's _way_ too much nuance to what's going on and even if they aren't technically affected, this kind of thing will almost surely make their paying enterprise customers leery.

Really frustrating that our privacy eroded to the point anyone would think this is reasonable.But it does explain some conversations with Gemini when I wonder why it's talking about particular things. Like asking it about consultation processes for changes to parks only to get a response that's uncannily tuned to the email I got prompting the enquiry.No mention of I just read your emails etc .

It's worse than that.> Google Photos data is used to infer your interests, relationships to people in your photos, and where you've been, including by associating your face with corresponding location data and timestamps. This data is also used to do things for you, like look up your info or add items to your grocery list, and to improve Google services, including training generative AI.How does that work exactly if the images aren't even real and are generated by AI? When Google siphons up these photos to help them train their AI, the AI is now going to make associations as depicted in that photograph?That you really were with that person, in that place, in that situation, on that date? As some sort of a fact?Can someone else create that image and just put it in their library and then have that become a fact on your behalf when picked up, analyzed and trained on?Where does that all lead?

I’ve had a chance to use fable 5.2. Some observations:- Anthropic is finally well balanced across models. Meaning: Opus 5.5 is so good that I do not feel Fable FOMO as I did when it was Fable 5/5.1 vs Opus 4.8/5. And Sonnet 5.5 sometimes makes me forget about Opus.- Fable is good, but you really have to push the ambition of your prompt in order to see proper separation from Opus 5.5. I personally have a hard time telling the difference between Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 for ordinary coding tasks.- It’s way faster and more reliable: one of the worst things about fable 5.1 was how slow it was an, on top of that, how frequently it would suffer from max output token overflows. I got none of these issues with 5.2.- Fable is exceptional at drawing. It’s ability to render an image with JavaScript actually has me questioning the value of dedicated image models. I prefer the images I’ve gotten fable/opus to make for me over those from gpt-image, it’s wild to think we’re at this point.

- Why are they stacking Fable xHigh against Carbon Med?- How did they produce such a bizarre effort-intel curve for Carbon that goes against every available benchmark?- Why did they leave Carbon-- positioned primarily as a cyber model-- off of the single cyber benchmark comparison?- Why do they switch to comparing against Argon (rather than carbon) for robodojo?

We've been early testing Fable 5.2, and have been surprised by its coding ability. It was able to work with an esoteric 600k line fortran codebase to speed up some computational material science work for us by 36 times (!). Given that this could be done in 2 days, we've decided to open-source the results https://github.com/discovered-materials/dm_qe

articles.title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
articles.summary: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs

top_comments: I wonder if this could be used anywhere as an alternative to Lloyd's algorithm. I have a hobby project which uses Lloyd's to "relax" an icosohedral equal area mesh on the surface of a sphere [1]. I'm going to try to swap it out with an adaptation of this and see if it's much better or if I can afford more iterations with this method.Edit: tried it, and it’s definitely not better for this use case. e-means wins by needing fewer passes over a huge dataset, but relaxing a mesh on a sphere has no dataset: each Voronoi cell’s centroid can be computed directly from its geometry. Mini-batches just swap that for a noisy sampled estimate of the same thing. It has the same objective and the same optimum, so at best it matches Lloyd. In practice it was much slower and left the grid noisy, and with small sample budgets it even tangled the mesh.[1] https://webgcm.app/explain/grid#nudging-the-cells-into-shape
I adapted the method to my IVF index (the code-daemon project) and achieved a 146x speedup on the GPU.That's impressive!

As far as I can tell this isn't particularly new, people have been doing minibatch k-means for a while, including with an EWA update. I assume the contribution here is that they tried to measure how much better it is and provided code? I'm not sure I agree with their claims though, because they didn't really measure the things that matter–sure, it's better than Lloyd's algorithm, but that's a very low bar.If you are claiming that your algorithm is "highly parallelizable" and comes with "wall-clock speedups", then the actual metrics that matter here is not number of steps or even basic wall clock time as your size remains fixed, but how your algorithm scales as more data is present or parallelism is required. This algorithm splits up the minibatch across workers and has them compute local updates, then allreduces it. As the amount of data goes up, the comms become much more expensive (since you have to use a worse transport layer), which means that you're basically locked in a desperate attempt to do more local work before you send your partial update to everyone else. If you attempt this (not explored in the paper) you will find that the improvement in clustering by doing this extra work has diminishing returns–you only reduce the number of updates by a few steps (which is what drives your wall clock time). At scale you end up being heavily comms limited and not super parallel at all.

articles.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
articles.summary: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game

top_comments: Growing up, games were such a scarce commodity that you'd really suck all the marrow out and spend hours beating your best times, looking for Easter eggs, or messing with custom maps and mods. There was a whole genre of gameplay around just exploiting physics bugs to jump a bit further.The other night I carelessly made an infinite runner game while watching TV and the feeling of sheer abundance quickly faded into a bit of depression. Without scarcity, nothing is really valuable.

I feel for kids growing up with LLMs like this. They will never impress a parent, teacher or peer with a simple “hello world” type text game, when the peer could generate a full multiplayer video game with a couple of prompts.The world has changed and we can never go back.

"one-shotting" is fun for a low (human) effort toy, but it's a mistake to get overly hung up on LLMs getting everything right on the first try, since a lot of that is the harness and the internal prompting that makes it burn extra tokens to test everything to get it in that one "shot" (ui turn).While it's nice that LLMs are getting better at arriving at the desired deliverable with fewer surprises (or broken things) doing it is not necessarily a sign that the model is actually smarter, just an indication that what you are doing is likely a well-trodden path for the model, the RL and the harness.

What surprises me with Infineon is that they seem to not work on a LLM on a chip. In particular that here in Linz Infineon, Apple's 5G modem designer and the Johannes Kepler University with Sepp Hochreiter (Inventor of LSTM) are just next to each other. I watched a interview of Infineon head of AI just recently, and I was like excited to hear about some cool hardware. And all he did is talk about how he uses LLMs.

Anyone know why it took so long for them to transition to 300mm? As mentioned in the article, they're mainly using existing 300mm equipment designed for silicon, which transitioned years ago. I imagine some process steps are different (mainly growing to larger boule, but probably others), but it doesn't seem like they would be huge blockers.

articles.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
articles.summary: Locating the source of a mysterious beep

top_comments: I didn't mention this in the article, but this isn't the first time my family has been driven almost spare by a mysterious, hard-to-track beep.Our dog goes outside and hides in the lavender bush if a smoke alarm starts making a "I need a battery" noise.So I went into this project with the attitude that I would like to solve this class of problem forever.

You can also solve this in O(logn) using a physical binary search:1) Move half the boxes to another room.2) Listen for a beep and determine which room the beep comes from.3) Take the boxes in that room and split them in half again.4) Repeat until one box is left.
Why didn't you time the interval between the beeps? Then when the next beep was coming up, just listen to a particular part of the room or set of boxes until you found it.
